analysis.one_liner: Caps U.S. prescription drug prices at the median price charged in eleven other wealthy countries.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with one cosponsor, was referred to six House committees and never received a markup or a vote before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Health and Human Services Secretary to set a maximum retail price for every prescription drug, based on the median list price in eleven reference countries such as Japan, Germany, France, and Canada. Those caps would apply to drugs bought under Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, TRICARE, VA care, the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program, and Indian Health Service programs [S2] [S3]. It would also require manufacturers to offer every drug at the reference price to uninsured people and to people with private insurance [S3]. Manufacturers that charged more would owe a civil penalty of five times the excess revenue, with the money transferred to the National Institutes of Health for drug research [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Seniors and disabled people on Medicare, families on Medicaid and CHIP, service members and veterans, federal employees, people served by the Indian Health Service, uninsured people who pay cash at the pharmacy, and people with private insurance would all gain access to drugs at internationally benchmarked prices [S2] [S3]. Taxpayers would also save, since federal programs pay much of the U.S. drug bill.

how_it_helps.text: Caps the retail list price of every covered drug at the median price in eleven reference countries, or, where pricing data is unavailable, at a price HHS judges appropriate based on the drug's value and development costs [S3].
Extends the capped price beyond federal programs: manufacturers must offer drugs at the reference price to uninsured individuals and to people covered by private or employer plans [S3].
Backs the cap with a civil penalty of five times the amount a manufacturer received above the reference price, and directs those penalty collections to NIH for drug research and development [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name and generic drug manufacturers, whose U.S. revenues would fall toward the lower prices charged in other wealthy countries; potentially lower industry research spending over time.

drawbacks.text: Lower U.S. revenue could reduce manufacturer investment in new drug research; the bill's own design, sending penalty collections to NIH for drug R&D, implicitly acknowledges this funding concern [S3].

For drugs unavailable in at least three reference countries, the price would rest on HHS's own judgment of therapeutic value and development cost, giving a federal agency wide pricing discretion [S3].
The cap applies to generic drugs as well as brand-name drugs, and generic margins are already thin, which could squeeze out some low-cost producers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete and immediate: lower drug prices for tens of millions of people, including the uninsured, in a country where drugs routinely cost several times what they cost in peer nations. The main cost is reduced pharmaceutical revenue and the possible knock-on to research investment; the bill tries to offset that by redirecting penalty revenue to NIH research. The design is broad and aggressive — covering generics and private buyers, not just federal programs — which is exactly what made it a heavy lift politically.

outcome.mechanism: Referred to six House committees and then to three subcommittees, but no committee ever acted on it, and it never came up for a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Peter Welch introduced the bill on April 22, 2021 [S1] [S5].

It was referred the same day to six committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Armed Services, Veterans' Affairs, Oversight and Reform, and Natural Resources — with jurisdiction to be determined later [S5].
Over the following months it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee, the Natural Resources Subcommittee for Indigenous Peoples, and another Health Subcommittee referral [S5].
No committee reported the bill, no hearing or markup is recorded, and no floor vote ever occurred before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmaceutical manufacturers, who kept charging U.S. patients and federal programs prices far above what the same drugs cost in other developed countries, with no cap enacted.

for.name: Rep. Peter Welch
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cap drug prices at international reference levels and referred it for committee consideration

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Health Subcommittee but never held a markup or moved it forward in the 117th Congress

against.name: House Ways and Means, Armed Services, Veterans' Affairs, Oversight and Reform, and Natural Resources Committees
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill after referral

against.name: Pharmaceutical industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed international reference pricing proposals as a leading lobbying presence while drug pricing bills were pending

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever recorded; sponsorship was Democratic only (Welch plus one Democratic cosponsor), and the record shows no stated Republican position either way [S4] [S5].

industries.note: The bill would cap their U.S. list prices at the median charged in eleven peer countries and apply that cap to every buyer, federal and private, with a five-times penalty for violations. This would end the pricing gap that lets them charge Americans far more than patients in other countries pay for the same drugs [S2] [S3].
Generic drugs are also subject to the reference price cap, which could squeeze thin margins in an already low-cost sector, though consumers would pay no more than before [S3].
The bill requires manufacturers to offer drugs at the reference price to people with private and employer coverage, lowering the drug costs that premiums and out-of-pocket charges are built on [S3].
